title: Guard Floor Openings and Stairwells During Framing
summary: A carpenter died after backing into an unguarded 6-foot stairwell opening and falling 19 feet to the basement. Guard every floor opening, check the work area each day, and know your emergency plan.
talking_points: A carpenter was cutting plywood on a second floor and handing it up to the roof. A sheet snagged in the trusses. While he pulled and repositioned it, he backed into an open stairwell and fell 19 feet. No steps or railings were in the opening.
Guard floor openings with railings. A standard railing has a top rail about 42 inches above the floor, a midrail halfway between, and a toeboard to keep tools and debris from falling in.
Open-sided floors and wall openings need the same kind of guarding.
Walk the work area with the crew each morning. Look for floor openings, loose debris, electrical hazards, and weather, then correct or avoid them. Do this again when work changes.
Watch your footing when you handle large sheets. Do not step backward without looking.
Have an emergency plan so help comes fast. In this case the owner drove about a mile to find a phone.
Employers should learn and follow OSHA standards, and they should have a safety program with fall hazard training.
site_hazards_to_check: Unguarded stairwell openings and floor holes
Work areas in a hallway or near openings where people back up while handling material
Large sheets that can snag on trusses and pull a worker off balance
No working phone or emergency plan at a rural site
discussion_questions: Which floor and stairwell openings are on this site, and how is each guarded?
What will you do if a sheet snags and you have to pull it free?
If someone is hurt here, who calls 911 and how do they give our location?
